title: Paul, the Letters and the Early Church
bigQuestion: How did a small movement, carried by travelers and letters, grow into a worldwide church with a fixed Bible and shared creeds?

story.title: A Letter Arrives in Corinth
story.kicker: Around 54 CE, a small community crowds into a house in a Greek port city to hear what its absent founder has written.
paragraphs: Imagine an evening in Corinth around the year 54. Corinth was a busy Roman port city on the narrow strip of land that joins mainland Greece to the south. Ships and goods passed through every day. In a large house, perhaps belonging to a man named Gaius, a few dozen people crowd into the dining room and the courtyard. Some are merchants. Some are enslaved workers who came after a long day. A few are Jews from the local synagogue. Most grew up worshiping the gods of Greece and Rome.

The wealthier guests have already eaten. By the time the workers arrive, the food is gone, and some early arrivals have had too much wine. There has been quarreling too. Some members say they belong to Paul, who founded the community. Others prefer Apollos, a gifted preacher who came later. Others name Cephas, the Aramaic name for Peter. People from the household of a woman named Chloe have carried news of these divisions across the sea to Paul, who is in Ephesus.

Tonight a letter has come back. Few people in the room can read, so one member stands and reads it aloud. It opens the way Greek letters did, with the sender's name: Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ. It greets the church of God at Corinth and wishes them grace and peace. Then it turns, gently at first and then sharply, to the quarrels. Is Christ divided, the letter asks. Was Paul crucified for you?

The reading goes on for a long time. It answers questions the Corinthians had sent in writing, about marriage, about meat offered to idols, about worship. It scolds them for the way they hold the Lord's Supper, when some go hungry while others feast. It compares the community to a body, where the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you. Then it slows into a passage about love: patient, kind, not proud, never failing.

No one recorded that evening. This scene is imagined, but its details come from the letter itself, which Christians call First Corinthians. Scholars date it to about 54 CE, earlier than any of the four Gospels. It is one of the oldest Christian writings that survive. When it was written, it was mail, sent to real people with real problems. This chapter asks how letters like it became part of a Bible that billions of people read today.
story.think: Paul wrote to solve problems in one community in one city. Why might Christians everywhere still read his letter as scripture? What changes when a piece of mail becomes a sacred text?

lessons.title: Pentecost in Jerusalem
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Acts tells how the followers of Jesus became a public movement in Jerusalem, beginning at the festival of Pentecost.
reading: The book of *Acts*, or the Acts of the Apostles, picks up where the Gospel of Luke stops. Both books address a man named Theophilus, and most scholars agree the same author wrote them. Luke told the story of Jesus. Acts tells the story of his followers over about thirty years. It moves from Jerusalem to Rome. It ends with Paul under guard in the capital of the empire, still preaching.

Acts, chapter 2, opens at *Pentecost*. This was the Jewish harvest festival of Shavuot, held fifty days after Passover. The name comes from the Greek word for fiftieth. Jews from across the empire had come to Jerusalem. According to Acts, the followers of Jesus were gathered in one place when a sound like wind filled the house. Something like tongues of fire rested on each of them. They began to speak in other languages, and visitors heard them in their own tongues.

Christians understand this as the coming of the *Holy Spirit*, the presence and power of God that Jesus had promised. Peter then speaks to the crowd. He quotes the prophet Joel and the Psalms, and he proclaims that God raised Jesus from the dead. Acts says about three thousand people were baptized that day. Many churches celebrate Pentecost each year, fifty days after Easter. Some call it the birthday of the church.

Acts then describes the first community in Jerusalem. Its members met daily in the Temple courts, broke bread in their homes, prayed and shared their goods so that no one was in need. Each leader was an *apostle*, a word meaning one who is sent. At this stage every follower was Jewish. The group did not see itself as a new religion. It saw itself as Jews who believed that Israel's Messiah had come. The question of outsiders was still ahead.

words.d: the fifth book of the New Testament, which tells how the followers of Jesus spread their message from Jerusalem to Rome
from the Greek for fiftieth; the Jewish harvest festival of Shavuot, and for Christians the day the Holy Spirit came, as told in Acts 2
in Christian belief, the presence and power of God at work in people and in the world
one who is sent; the name for Jesus' closest followers and for leaders such as Paul who spread the message

look.title: Many Languages, One Message
look.text: Acts, chapter 2, lists the places the pilgrims in Jerusalem came from: Parthia, Media, Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Egypt, Libya, Rome, Crete, Arabia and more. Each person, Acts says, heard the followers of Jesus speaking in his own language. The writer names the lands one by one instead of simply saying that many people were there.
look.prompt: Why might the author of Acts take the time to name so many places? What does this opening scene suggest about where the rest of the book is going?

check.q: Which Gospel was written by the same author as Acts, according to most scholars?
choices: Luke
Mark
John
Matthew
check.why: Both Luke and Acts are addressed to Theophilus, and most scholars agree one author wrote both books.

check.q: What was Pentecost before it became a Christian holiday?
choices: A Roman festival honoring the emperor
The Jewish harvest festival of Shavuot, fifty days after Passover
The day the Temple was destroyed
A Greek athletic contest
check.why: Pentecost means fiftieth; it was the Jewish festival of Shavuot, which brought pilgrims to Jerusalem.

check.q: How did the first followers in Jerusalem see themselves, according to the reading?
choices: As members of a new religion separate from Judaism
As Roman citizens loyal to the emperor
As Jews who believed Israel's Messiah had come
As Samaritans who worshiped on Mount Gerizim
check.why: Every early follower was Jewish, and the group saw itself as Jews who believed the Messiah had come.

lessons.title: Saul Becomes Paul
lessons.mainIdea: Paul, a Jewish Pharisee who once opposed the followers of Jesus, became their most influential missionary after an experience on the road to Damascus.
reading: Acts introduces Paul under his Hebrew name, Saul. He first appears at the stoning of Stephen, whom Christians honor as the first *martyr*, holding the cloaks of the men who threw the stones. In his own letters Paul calls himself a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin and a Pharisee, zealous for the law. He was born in Tarsus, a city in what is now southern Turkey. Acts adds that he was a Roman citizen. He also used the Roman name Paul, and Acts calls him Saul, who is also called Paul.

Paul says plainly that he persecuted the church. Then something changed. Acts, chapter 9, tells the story. Saul is traveling to Damascus with letters to arrest followers of Jesus. A light from heaven flashes around him. He falls to the ground and hears a voice asking why he persecutes him. The voice says it is Jesus. Saul rises blind and is led into the city. Three days later a follower named Ananias lays hands on him. His sight returns, and he is baptized.

Christians call this Paul's *conversion*, a turning to a new faith. Some scholars prefer the word call. In Galatians, chapter 1, Paul describes the event the way the prophets described their calling. He says God revealed his Son to him so that he might preach among the *Gentiles*, the non-Jewish peoples. Paul never stopped seeing himself as a Jew. What changed was his belief about Jesus and about who belonged to God's people.

Acts tells the Damascus story three times, in chapters 9, 22 and 26, with small differences in detail. That repetition shows how important the author thought it was. Paul's own account in Galatians is shorter. He adds that he went to Arabia, returned to Damascus, and waited three years before visiting Peter in Jerusalem. Comparing the two accounts practices a skill from this course: the same event, told by two writers for two purposes.

words.d: a person who is killed because of his or her faith; Christians honor Stephen as the first Christian martyr
a turning from one way of life or belief to another; used for Paul's change on the road to Damascus
people who are not Jewish; Paul saw his mission as bringing the message about Jesus to them

look.title: On the Road to Damascus
look.text: And as he journeyed, he came near Damascus: and suddenly there shined round about him a light from heaven: And he fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?
look.prompt: The voice does not ask why Saul persecutes the church. It asks why he persecutes me. What does that wording suggest about how Acts connects Jesus with his followers?

check.q: What was Paul's background before he followed Jesus, according to his own letters?
choices: A Roman soldier stationed in Damascus
A Samaritan priest
A fisherman from Galilee
A Jewish Pharisee from the tribe of Benjamin
check.why: Paul describes himself as a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin and a Pharisee, zealous for the law.

check.q: What does the word Gentiles mean?
choices: People who are not Jewish
Jewish teachers of the law
Roman governors
Followers of John the Baptist
check.why: Gentiles are non-Jewish peoples; Paul says God called him to preach among them.

check.q: Why do some scholars prefer to call Paul's experience a call rather than a conversion?
choices: Because Paul never went to Damascus
Because Paul describes it the way the prophets described their calling and still saw himself as a Jew
Because Acts never mentions it
Because Paul had followed Jesus since childhood
check.why: In Galatians 1 Paul uses the language of a prophet's call, and he never stopped seeing himself as a Jew.

lessons.title: Journeys and the Jerusalem Council
lessons.mainIdea: Paul's journeys planted churches in Roman cities, and a meeting in Jerusalem decided that Gentile believers did not have to become Jews first.
reading: Acts describes Paul setting out from Antioch in Syria, a large city where, Acts says, the followers were first called Christians. Scholars often divide his travels into three trips, plus a final voyage to Rome. Each trip is called a *missionary journey*. He went to Cyprus and the cities of what is now Turkey. Then he crossed into Greece: Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens and Corinth, where he stayed a year and a half. Later he spent more than two years in Ephesus. He usually worked with partners such as Barnabas, Silas and Timothy.

Acts shows a pattern. Paul goes first to the local synagogue and speaks to Jews and to Gentiles who attended it. Some accept his message and some reject it. Then he teaches in homes and public places. He supported himself by making tents, so he would not be a burden. Small communities formed and met in homes. When Paul moved on, he stayed in touch through visits, co-workers and letters.

As Gentiles joined, a hard question arose. Did a Gentile man have to be circumcised and keep the whole Torah to belong? The ritual of *circumcision* was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham in Genesis 17. Some Jewish believers said yes. Paul and Barnabas said no. According to Acts, chapter 15, the apostles and elders met in Jerusalem around 49 CE to decide. Scholars call this meeting the *Council of Jerusalem*. Peter spoke, and James, the leader of the Jerusalem church, gave the decision.

The council decided that Gentile believers did not need to be circumcised. It asked them to avoid a few things: food offered to idols, blood, the meat of strangled animals and sexual immorality. That choice opened the movement to the wider Roman world. It did not settle every argument, as Paul's letter to the Galatians shows. Acts ends with Paul arrested in Jerusalem, appealing to the emperor and sent to Rome. Early Christian tradition holds that he was executed there under Nero in the 60s.

words.d: one of Paul's trips to spread the message about Jesus and start communities in the cities of the Roman Empire
a ritual cutting of the foreskin; in Genesis 17, the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and his descendants
the meeting of apostles and elders described in Acts 15, around 49 CE, that decided Gentile believers need not be circumcised

look.title: The Council's Question
look.text: A Greek merchant in Corinth has heard Paul preach and wants to join the community. He has never kept the Sabbath, eats pork and has never entered a synagogue. One group of Jewish believers says he must be circumcised and keep the Torah like any convert to Judaism. Paul says faith in Christ is enough.
look.prompt: Using Acts 15, explain what the Council of Jerusalem decided for someone like this merchant. What did it still ask him to avoid, and why might those limits have mattered for shared meals with Jewish believers?

check.q: In which city were the followers first called Christians, according to Acts?
choices: Jerusalem
Rome
Antioch
Corinth
check.why: Acts says the disciples were first called Christians in Antioch in Syria, where Paul's journeys began.

check.q: What question did the Council of Jerusalem decide?
choices: Whether Paul could visit Rome
Which Gospel to read in worship
Whether the Temple should be rebuilt
Whether Gentile believers had to be circumcised and keep the whole Torah
check.why: Acts 15 says the council decided Gentile believers did not need to be circumcised.

check.q: How did Paul usually begin his work in a new city, according to Acts?
choices: By speaking in the local synagogue
By meeting the Roman governor
By building a church
By writing a Gospel
check.why: Acts shows Paul going first to the synagogue, where he spoke to Jews and to Gentiles who attended.

lessons.title: How an Ancient Letter Works
lessons.mainIdea: Paul's letters are real ancient letters, written to particular churches about particular problems, and they are the oldest writings in the New Testament.
reading: Open any of Paul's letters and look at the first lines. They follow the pattern of Greek letters of the time. First comes the sender: Paul, sometimes with a co-worker such as Timothy. Then come the readers: the church of God at Corinth, or the churches of Galatia. Then a greeting. Where a Greek letter said greetings, Paul says grace to you and peace. A thanksgiving usually follows, then the main body, then advice, travel plans and personal greetings at the end.

The New Testament contains thirteen letters that bear Paul's name. The Greek word for letter gives us *epistle*, the older English name for them. Most scholars agree Paul wrote seven: Romans, First and Second Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, First Thessalonians and Philemon. The other six are debated. Many scholars think followers wrote some of them in his name after his death, a common practice in the ancient world. Many Christians hold that Paul wrote all thirteen. First Thessalonians, from about 50 CE, is probably the oldest surviving Christian writing.

Paul did not usually write with his own hand. He dictated to a *scribe*, a trained writer. In Romans 16 the scribe, Tertius, adds his own greeting. At the end of Galatians, Paul takes the pen himself and points out the large letters of his own handwriting. Trusted co-workers carried the letters by road and ship. Then they read them aloud to the gathered community.

Those communities were *house churches*. There were no church buildings yet. Believers met in the homes of members who had room, such as Prisca and Aquila, a couple Paul names more than once. A letter was read to everyone at once, enslaved and free, women and men. That is why reading Paul is like hearing one side of a phone call. He answers questions and problems that we must reconstruct from his replies.

words.d: a letter; the older English name for the letters in the New Testament
a trained writer who wrote down what someone else dictated; Paul used scribes such as Tertius
early Christian communities that met in the homes of members, before there were church buildings

look.title: Paul's Undisputed Letters by Length
look.cite: Standard New Testament chapter divisions; the seven letters most scholars agree Paul wrote
look.prompt: Philemon is a single chapter, a personal note about one enslaved man. Romans has sixteen. What might explain such different lengths? Which letter would you read first to meet Paul, and why?

check.q: How many letters in the New Testament bear Paul's name?
choices: Four
Thirteen
Seven
Twenty-seven
check.why: Thirteen letters bear Paul's name; most scholars agree he wrote seven of them.

check.q: What is probably the oldest surviving Christian writing?
choices: The Gospel of Mark
The book of Revelation
Paul's First Letter to the Thessalonians, from about 50 CE
The Nicene Creed
check.why: First Thessalonians, written about 50 CE, is older than any Gospel.

check.q: Why is reading Paul like hearing one side of a phone call?
choices: Because his letters were spoken, never written
Because he wrote in a secret code
Because every original letter was lost
Because he answers questions and problems that readers must reconstruct from his replies
check.why: Paul wrote to real communities about their questions, which we know mainly through his answers.

lessons.title: Faith and Grace in Romans and Galatians
lessons.mainIdea: In Romans and Galatians, Paul teaches that people are put right with God through faith and God's grace, a teaching Christians interpret in different ways.
reading: Galatians is Paul's angriest letter. He skips the usual thanksgiving. Teachers had come to Galatia, in what is now central Turkey, telling Gentile believers they must be circumcised. Paul answers that a person is put right with God not by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. He even describes confronting Peter at Antioch for pulling away from meals with Gentile believers. For Paul, shared tables showed that Jews and Gentiles now belonged to one family.

Romans, written about 57 CE to a church Paul had not yet visited, lays out the argument more calmly. It is his longest letter. He argues that all people, Jew and Gentile, have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. God's answer, he says, is *grace*, a gift that cannot be earned. The Greek word he uses for being put right with God is usually translated *justification*. It is received through *faith*, which for Paul means trust and loyalty, not only agreement with ideas.

These chapters changed later history. In 386 Augustine, a teacher from North Africa, read a verse from Romans 13 in a garden in Milan and turned to Christianity. In the 1500s the German monk Martin Luther read Romans and Galatians as teaching justification by faith alone, a key idea of the Protestant Reformation. In 1738 John Wesley, who founded Methodism, felt his heart strangely warmed while hearing Luther's preface to Romans read in London.

Christians do not all read these letters the same way. Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that faith works together with love and the life of the church. It points to the Letter of James, which says that faith without works is dead. Protestants have read James as describing faith that shows itself in action. Since the late twentieth century, many scholars have argued that Paul's main concern was whether Gentiles could belong without becoming Jews. That view is called the New Perspective on Paul.

words.d: in Christian teaching, God's free gift of love and favor, which cannot be earned
being put right with God; Paul teaches that it comes through faith
in Paul's letters, trust in and loyalty to God and Christ, not only agreement with ideas

look.title: Peace Through Faith
look.text: Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:
look.prompt: The word therefore shows that this verse sums up an argument. Using the reading, explain in your own words what Paul says has happened and how. How might a Catholic reader and a Lutheran reader explain the verse differently?

check.q: What problem caused Paul to write Galatians?
choices: Teachers were telling Gentile believers they must be circumcised
The church had no place to meet
Roman soldiers had closed the synagogue
The Galatians wanted a new Gospel written
check.why: In Galatians Paul argues against teachers who said Gentile believers must be circumcised.

check.q: What does Paul mean by grace?
choices: A reward for keeping the law perfectly
A gift from God that cannot be earned
A prayer said before meals
A Roman legal document
check.why: In Romans, grace is God's free gift, received through faith rather than earned.

check.q: Which reformer read Romans and Galatians as teaching justification by faith alone?
choices: Augustine
Irenaeus
Martin Luther
Constantine
check.why: Martin Luther's reading of these letters became a key idea of the Protestant Reformation.

lessons.title: Love and the Body in Corinth
lessons.mainIdea: First Corinthians answers a divided church by describing it as one body and naming love as the greatest gift.
reading: Corinth's church had many problems, and First Corinthians takes them one at a time. Members quarreled over leaders. Some treated the Lord's Supper as an ordinary dinner party, where the wealthy ate first and the poor went hungry. Paul answers by repeating what he says he received. On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus took bread and said, this is my body. Written around 54 CE, this is the oldest surviving account of the Last Supper, older than any Gospel.

In chapter 12 Paul uses a picture that Greek and Roman writers used for a city: a body. He applies it to the church, which he calls the *body of Christ*. The foot cannot say it does not belong because it is not a hand. The eye cannot tell the hand it is not needed. Each member has a different gift, such as teaching, healing or helping. The weaker parts, Paul says, deserve special honor.

Chapter 13 follows, and it is one of the most read passages in the Bible. Paul says that speaking in tongues, prophecy and even giving everything away are worth nothing without love. Love is patient and kind. It is not jealous, boastful or rude. The Greek word is *agape*, a self-giving love. The King James Version translates it as *charity*, which in 1611 could mean love in this full sense. Modern translations say love. The chapter is often read at weddings, though Paul wrote it to a quarreling congregation.

Other chapters deal with marriage, with meat that had been sacrificed to Greek gods and then sold in the market, and with order in worship. Chapter 15 contains the early summary of the resurrection belief that you met in the last chapter. First Corinthians shows how Paul's theology grew out of practical questions. He rarely wrote abstract theology for its own sake. He wrote to help a real community live together.

words.d: Paul's picture of the church as one body with many members, each with a different gift
a Greek word for self-giving love, the love Paul describes in First Corinthians 13
in the King James Version, the word used to translate agape, meaning love in its fullest sense

look.title: Faith, Hope and Love
look.text: And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
look.prompt: Here charity means love, translating the Greek agape. Why might Paul rank love above faith and hope when writing to a divided church? How does this verse connect to his picture of the body in chapter 12?

check.q: What does Paul call the church in First Corinthians 12?
choices: The new Temple of Herod
The kingdom of Rome
The house of Israel
The body of Christ
check.why: Paul compares the church to a body with many members and calls it the body of Christ.

check.q: What does the word charity mean in the King James Version of First Corinthians 13?
choices: Love, translating the Greek word agape
Giving money to the poor, and nothing more
A church tax
A kind of prayer
check.why: The King James Version uses charity for agape, which modern translations render as love.

check.q: Why is Paul's account of the Last Supper in First Corinthians important to historians?
choices: It is the only account of the meal
It is older than any of the Gospel accounts
It was written by Jesus
It was found among the Dead Sea Scrolls
check.why: First Corinthians dates to about 54 CE, before any Gospel was written.

lessons.title: Revelation and Apocalyptic Writing
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation is apocalyptic writing, full of symbols and visions, which Christians have read as a message about suffering, hope and the end of history.
reading: The last book of the New Testament begins with a man named John on Patmos, a small island off the coast of what is now Turkey. He says he was there because of his witness to Jesus. He sees visions and writes them down for seven churches in the Roman province of Asia, including Ephesus and Smyrna. Many scholars date the book to about 95 CE, near the end of the emperor Domitian's reign. Christians have long debated whether this John was the apostle or another John.

The book belongs to a genre scholars call *apocalyptic*, from the Greek apokalypsis, meaning unveiling or revealing. Apocalyptic writing uses dreams, angels, strange beasts and numbers to reveal a hidden meaning in history. The book of Daniel in the Hebrew Bible is an earlier example. Several other Jewish apocalypses were written in the same centuries. First readers knew how to read the images, the way we read a political cartoon.

Revelation is dense with *symbols*. A lamb that was slain stands for Christ. Seven is a number of completeness. A beast rises from the sea, and a woman called Babylon rides on a beast. Many scholars read Babylon as a code name for Rome, the empire that ruled and at times persecuted Christians. The book ends with a new heaven and a new earth, and a *new Jerusalem* where God lives with people and wipes away every tear.

Christians have read Revelation in several ways. Some read it mainly as a message to churches under pressure in John's own time. Some read it as a forecast of events still to come at the end of history. Many read it as a symbolic picture of the struggle between good and evil in every age. Its place in the Bible was debated for centuries, especially in the East. Eastern Orthodox churches still do not include it among the readings at their main Sunday service.

words.d: a kind of writing that uses visions, symbols and angels to reveal hidden meaning in history and its end
images that stand for something else, such as the lamb in Revelation standing for Christ
in Revelation, the holy city of the renewed world, where God lives among people

look.title: A New Heaven and a New Earth
look.text: And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.
look.prompt: List the things this verse says will end. Why might this promise have mattered to small communities under pressure from a powerful empire? How is its tone different from the visions of beasts earlier in the book?

check.q: What does the Greek word apokalypsis mean?
choices: Destruction
Final battle
Unveiling or revealing
Letter
check.why: Apocalyptic comes from apokalypsis, an unveiling of hidden meaning, not simply destruction.

check.q: Which book of the Hebrew Bible is an earlier example of apocalyptic writing?
choices: Leviticus
Ruth
Proverbs
Daniel
check.why: Daniel uses visions and symbolic beasts, as Revelation later does.

check.q: What do many scholars think Babylon stands for in Revelation?
choices: Rome
Jerusalem
Egypt
Athens
check.why: Many scholars read Babylon as a code name for Rome, the empire that ruled John's readers.

lessons.title: How the Canon Formed
lessons.mainIdea: The New Testament's twenty-seven books were gathered over about three centuries as churches decided which writings to read as scripture.
reading: In 367 CE Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria in Egypt, sent his yearly Easter letter to the churches under his care. In it he listed the books to be read as scripture. His list of twenty-seven New Testament books is the earliest known list that matches today's exactly. By then Christians had been reading many of these writings for nearly three hundred years. The list recorded a long process more than it started one.

A *canon* is an official list of sacred books. The word comes from a Greek word for a measuring rod or rule. In the second century a teacher named Marcion, active in Rome around 140, rejected the Hebrew Bible. He accepted only an edited Luke and ten of Paul's letters. Other church leaders rejected his short list. Around 180 the bishop Irenaeus defended exactly four Gospels. Debates like these pushed churches to say clearly which books they held in common.

Scholars describe three main tests that early Christians used. Was a book connected to an apostle or to someone close to one? Was it widely read in worship across many churches? Did it agree with what the churches already taught? The four Gospels and Paul's letters were accepted early. Hebrews, James, Second Peter, Jude and Revelation were *disputed* for longer. Other popular writings, such as the Shepherd of Hermas, were read in some churches but finally left out.

Early Christians also favored a newer kind of book. Instead of scrolls, they copied their texts in the *codex*, a book of pages bound along one edge, like books today. A codex could hold all four Gospels or all of Paul's letters in one volume. Church councils in North Africa, at Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397, affirmed the same twenty-seven books. Almost all churches today accept this New Testament.

words.d: from a Greek word for a measuring rod; the official list of books a community accepts as scripture
in the history of the canon, books whose place in scripture was debated for a long time before most churches accepted them
a book made of pages bound along one edge, which early Christians preferred to the scroll

look.title: What Is in the New Testament
look.cite: Standard New Testament contents, matching the list Athanasius gave in 367 CE
look.prompt: Letters make up 21 of the 27 books. What does that suggest about how the early churches kept in touch? Why might churches have kept four Gospels instead of blending them into one?

check.q: What is a canon?
choices: A church building
An official list of sacred books
A Roman law about religion
A type of prayer
check.why: A canon, from a Greek word for a measuring rod, is the list of books a community accepts as scripture.

check.q: Who wrote the earliest known list that matches today's twenty-seven New Testament books?
choices: Marcion, around 140
Paul, around 50
Athanasius of Alexandria, in 367
Martin Luther, in 1517
check.why: Athanasius listed exactly the twenty-seven books in his Easter letter of 367 CE.

check.q: Why did early Christians favor the codex over the scroll, according to the reading?
choices: Scrolls were forbidden by Roman law
A codex could not be copied
Only Jews were allowed to use scrolls
A codex could hold several books, such as all four Gospels, in one volume
check.why: The codex, with bound pages, could gather many writings into one book.

lessons.title: The Creeds
lessons.mainIdea: Creeds are short statements of belief that early church councils wrote to settle disputes, and the Nicene Creed is still recited by most Christians.
reading: Stand in a Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran or Anglican service on a Sunday and you will likely hear the congregation speak together: we believe in one God, the Father, the Almighty, maker of heaven and earth. These are the opening words of the *Nicene Creed*. A *creed*, from the Latin credo, meaning I believe, is a summary of faith that believers say together. The earliest creeds grew out of the questions asked of new members at baptism.

The Nicene Creed came out of a crisis. Around 318 a priest in Alexandria named Arius taught that the Son of God was created by the Father and so was not fully God. Others, including the young Athanasius, argued that the Son was fully divine. In 325 the emperor Constantine, who had ended the persecution of Christians, called bishops to the city of Nicaea to settle the matter. The council declared the Son to be of one substance with the Father. A council at Constantinople in 381 expanded the creed.

The creeds state the doctrine of the *Trinity*: one God in three persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The word Trinity does not appear in the Bible. Christian thinkers developed it to describe what they believed the scriptures taught. In the West, the shorter Apostles' Creed, which grew from an early baptismal creed used in Rome, is also widely used. Most Christians today accept the Nicene teaching. A few groups that identify as Christian, such as Jehovah's Witnesses and Unitarians, do not.

The creeds also show how Christians read the whole Bible as one story. God creates. The Son becomes human, suffers under Pontius Pilate, rises and will come again. The Spirit gives life. A single phrase later divided East and West. Western churches added a line saying the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Eastern churches objected, and the dispute became one cause of the split between them in 1054.

words.d: the statement of Christian belief from the Council of Nicaea (325), expanded at Constantinople (381), still recited by most churches
from the Latin credo, I believe; a short summary of faith that believers say together
the Christian teaching that God is one God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit

look.title: From the Nicene Creed
look.text: We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth. We believe in one Lord, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, true God from true God, of one being with the Father. He became human, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, rose on the third day and will come again. We believe in the Holy Spirit, the giver of life.
look.cite: Nicene Creed, Council of Nicaea (325) as expanded at Constantinople (381); shortened and in our own words
look.prompt: Which phrase answers the question Arius raised? Find it and explain how it settles his claim. Why might a creed about God name a Roman governor, Pontius Pilate?

check.q: What does the Latin word credo mean?
choices: I believe
I pray
I am sent
Good news
check.why: Creed comes from credo, I believe, because a creed states what believers hold together.

check.q: What question did the Council of Nicaea in 325 try to settle?
choices: Whether Gentiles had to be circumcised
Whether the Son was fully divine or created by the Father, as Arius taught
Whether Paul wrote Hebrews
Whether Revelation belonged in the canon
check.why: Nicaea answered Arius by declaring the Son to be of one substance with the Father.

check.q: What does the doctrine of the Trinity state?
choices: That there are three separate gods
That Jesus was only a prophet
That God is one God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit
That the Holy Spirit is an angel
check.why: The creeds teach one God in three persons, a teaching most Christians accept.

lessons.title: Reading the Old Through the New
lessons.mainIdea: Christians read the Hebrew Bible as the Old Testament, interpreting it through Jesus, while Jews read the same books as a complete scripture on their own terms.
reading: In First Corinthians 5, Paul writes that Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. He takes a practice from Exodus, the lamb whose blood marked Israelite doors, and reads it as pointing to Jesus. This way of reading is called *typology*. A person or event in the earlier scriptures is seen as a type, a pattern or foreshadowing, of Christ. Early Christian writers used typology often. Adam, Isaac and Jonah were all read as types.

For this reason Christians call the Hebrew scriptures the *Old Testament*. Testament means covenant. The name draws on the prophet Jeremiah, who spoke of a new covenant, and on New Testament passages that quote him. Christians hold that the two testaments form one Bible, with the New as the key to the Old. The Gospels often say that something happened to fulfill what the prophets said. Christians read Isaiah 53, about a servant who suffers for others, as a picture of Jesus.

Jews read the same books differently, as a complete scripture, the Tanakh, not as the older part of something else. Jewish interpreters have often read the suffering servant of Isaiah as the people of Israel. Jewish tradition does not hold that Jesus fulfilled the prophecies about the Messiah. The two traditions share a text and read it through different lenses: Christians through the New Testament, Jews through the rabbis and the Talmud. For this reason, many scholars say Hebrew Bible when describing the shared books.

This difference had real consequences. For many centuries some Christians taught that the church had simply replaced Israel as God's people, a view scholars call *supersessionism*. That teaching fed hostility toward Jews. After the Holocaust, many churches reexamined it. In 1965 the Catholic Church's document Nostra Aetate stated that Jews as a people should not be blamed for the death of Jesus. It also affirmed the bond between Christians and Jews. Many Protestant churches have issued similar statements.

words.d: a way of reading in which a person or event in the earlier scriptures is seen as a pattern pointing to Christ
the Christian name for the Hebrew scriptures; testament means covenant
the view that the church replaced Israel as God's people, which many churches have rejected or revised since the Holocaust

look.title: One Passage, Two Readings
look.text: Isaiah 53 describes a servant who is despised and rejected, who carries the sorrows of others and is wounded for their wrongdoing. Christian readers from the New Testament onward have read this servant as Jesus. Many Jewish readers, including the medieval commentator Rashi, have read the servant as the people of Israel, suffering among the nations.
look.prompt: Both readings take the text seriously. What does each tradition bring to the passage that shapes its reading? How can a student describe both fairly without deciding between them?

check.q: What is typology?
choices: A way of dating ancient manuscripts
The study of Greek grammar
A list of the books in the canon
Reading an earlier person or event as a pattern that points to Christ
check.why: Paul's reading of the Passover lamb as Christ is an example of typology.

check.q: How do Jews generally read the books Christians call the Old Testament?
choices: As a complete scripture, the Tanakh, read through the rabbis and the Talmud
As the first half of the Christian Bible
As books with no religious meaning
As a later addition to the New Testament
check.why: For Jews the Tanakh is complete in itself and is interpreted through rabbinic tradition.

check.q: What did the Catholic document Nostra Aetate (1965) state?
choices: That the New Testament canon was closed
That Jews as a people should not be blamed for the death of Jesus
That Paul wrote Hebrews
That Easter must fall on one date
check.why: Nostra Aetate rejected blaming Jews as a people and affirmed the bond between Christians and Jews.

lessons.title: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant
lessons.mainIdea: Christianity today has three large branches, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, shaped by the split of 1054 and the Reformation that began in 1517.
reading: On Chicago's Near North Side, Holy Name Cathedral is the seat of the Catholic archbishop. In the Ukrainian Village neighborhood, Holy Trinity Cathedral, designed by the architect Louis Sullivan, serves an Orthodox congregation. Across the city stand Lutheran, Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian and Pentecostal churches. All of them read the New Testament that this chapter has traced. They differ over authority, worship and how to read those texts.

The *Catholic* Church, led by the bishop of Rome, the pope, is the largest branch, with more than a billion members. The *Orthodox* churches, strongest in Greece, Eastern Europe and the Middle East, are a family of self-governing churches led by patriarchs and bishops. East and West had grown apart for centuries over language, customs and the authority of the pope. In 1054 leaders in Rome and Constantinople excommunicated each other. That event is often called the Great *Schism*, though the break hardened slowly.

In 1517 a German monk, Martin Luther, published ninety-five theses criticizing the sale of indulgences, grants said to lessen punishment for sin. His protest grew into the *Reformation*. Protestants taught that scripture alone is the final authority and that people are justified by grace through faith alone. The movement soon divided into many churches: Lutheran, Reformed and Presbyterian, Anglican, Baptist, and later Methodist and Pentecostal. The Catholic Church answered with its own reforms at the Council of Trent, which met between 1545 and 1563.

The branches read the same New Testament but differ in emphasis. Catholics and Orthodox give great weight to tradition and to sacraments such as baptism and the Eucharist. Orthodox worship centers on the Divine Liturgy and on icons, painted images of Christ and the saints. Most *Protestant* churches stress preaching and personal Bible reading. Their Bibles differ too. Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments include several books, such as Tobit and the Maccabees, that most Protestants call the Apocrypha. In 1965 Rome and Constantinople lifted their excommunications of 1054.

words.d: the branch of Christianity led by the pope, the bishop of Rome; the largest Christian church
the family of self-governing Eastern churches led by patriarchs and bishops, strongest in Greece, Eastern Europe and the Middle East
a formal split within a religious community; the Great Schism of 1054 divided Rome and Constantinople
the movement that began with Martin Luther in 1517 and produced the Protestant churches
the churches that came from the Reformation, which teach that scripture alone is the final authority

check.q: What happened in 1054?
choices: Luther published ninety-five theses
The Council of Nicaea met
Leaders in Rome and Constantinople excommunicated each other
Athanasius listed the New Testament books
check.why: The mutual excommunications of 1054 are often called the Great Schism between East and West.

check.q: Which teaching is a key Protestant idea from the Reformation?
choices: The pope is the final authority
Only Orthodox churches may use icons
The Trinity should be rejected
Scripture alone is the final authority, and people are justified by faith
check.why: Luther and other reformers taught scripture alone and justification by grace through faith.

check.q: How do Catholic and Protestant Bibles differ?
choices: Catholic Old Testaments include several books, such as Tobit and Maccabees, that most Protestants call the Apocrypha
Protestant Bibles have no New Testament
Catholic Bibles leave out the Gospels
Protestant Bibles leave out Paul's letters
check.why: The New Testaments match; the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments include extra books.

review.q: According to Acts 2, what happened at Pentecost?
choices: Paul was shipwrecked on Malta
The followers of Jesus received the Holy Spirit and Peter preached to crowds in Jerusalem
The Council of Jerusalem met
Jesus entered Jerusalem on a donkey
review.why: Acts 2 places the coming of the Holy Spirit and Peter's speech at the Jewish festival of Pentecost.

review.q: Which statement about Paul is accurate?
choices: He was one of the twelve disciples in Galilee
He wrote all four Gospels
He was a Pharisee who persecuted the church before his experience on the road to Damascus
He was a Roman governor of Judea
review.why: Paul calls himself a Pharisee who persecuted the church; Acts 9 tells of his experience near Damascus.

review.q: Which of these is one of the seven letters most scholars agree Paul wrote?
choices: Hebrews
First Timothy
Revelation
Galatians
review.why: Galatians is among the seven undisputed letters; Hebrews is anonymous and First Timothy is debated.

review.q: What is the main idea of Paul's picture of the body of Christ?
choices: The church is one community with many members who need each other
Only leaders matter in the church
The church is a building
Believers should leave their cities
review.why: In First Corinthians 12 each member has a different gift, and none can say it has no need of another.

review.q: How is Revelation best described as a genre?
choices: A letter of advice about marriage
Apocalyptic writing that uses visions and symbols
A law code like Leviticus
A biography of Paul
review.why: Revelation, like Daniel, is apocalyptic: it unveils hidden meaning through visions and symbols.

review.q: Why did early churches need to settle the canon?
choices: Rome ordered them to burn their books
There were no Christian writings before 367
Teachers such as Marcion proposed different lists, and churches needed a shared scripture
Paul asked them to in Romans
review.why: Marcion's short list and other debates pushed churches to name the books they held in common.

review.q: What did the Nicene Creed affirm against the teaching of Arius?
choices: That the Holy Spirit is a created being
That Jesus was only a teacher
That Gentiles need not be circumcised
That the Son is of one substance with the Father
review.why: Arius said the Son was created; Nicaea declared him of one substance with the Father.

review.q: Which pair of events shaped the three main branches of Christianity?
choices: The split of 1054 and the Reformation that began in 1517
The Council of Jerusalem and Pentecost
The writing of Romans and of Revelation
The founding of Antioch and of Corinth
review.why: 1054 divided Catholic and Orthodox; the Reformation of 1517 produced the Protestant churches.
